#Text=Next in order of delicacy, and more closely allied with the physical
#Text= functions, is the sense of smell.
#Text=Delicate perfumes, or the fragrance of
#Text= a flower, impart an exhilarating sensation of delight, while numerous
#Text= odors excite a feeling of disgust.
#Text=The organ of smell is far less
#Text= complicated in its structure than the eye or the ear.
#Text=It consists of two
#Text=cavities having cartilaginous walls, and lined with a thick mucous coat,
#Text= termed the _pituitary membrane_, over which are reflected the olfactory
#Text= nerves.
#Text=Particles of matter, too minute to be visible even through the
#Text= microscope, are detached from the odorous body and come in contact with
#Text= the nerves of smell, which transmit the impressions or impulses thus
#Text= received to the brain.
#Text=Fig. 65 shows the distribution of the olfactory
#Text= nerves in the nasal passages.
#Text=The nose is supplied with two kinds of
#Text= filaments which are termed respectively nerves of _special_ and nerves
#Text= of _general sensation_.
#Text=Compared with the lower animals, especially with
#Text= those belonging to the carnivorous species, the sense of smell in man is
#Text= feeble.
#Text=The sensation of smell is especially connected with the
#Text= pleasures and necessities of animal life.
#Text=TASTE.
#Text=The sense of taste is directly connected with the preservation and
#Text= nutrition of the body.
#Text=A delicious flavor produces a desire to eat a
#Text= savory substance.
#Text=Some writers on hygiene have given this sense an
#Text=instinctive character, by assuming that all articles having an agreeable
#Text= taste are suitable for diet.
#Text=The nerves of taste are distributed over
#Text= the surface of the tongue and palate, and their minute extremities
#Text= terminate in well developed _papillae_.
#Text=These _papillae_ are divided
#Text= into three classes, termed, from their microscopic appearance,
#Text= _filiform_, _fungiform_ and _circumvallate_.
#Text=The organ of taste is the
#Text= mucous membrane which covers the back part of the tongue and the palate.
#Text=The papillae of the tongue are large and distinct, and covered with
#Text= separate coats of epithelium.
#Text=The filiform papillae are generally long
#Text= and pointed and are found over the entire surface of the tongue.
#Text=The
#Text= fungiform are longer, small at the base and broad at the end.
#Text=The
#Text= circumvallate are shaped like an inverted V and are found only near the
#Text= root of the tongue; the largest of this class of papillae have other
#Text= very small papillae upon their surfaces.
#Text=It is now pretty satisfactorily
#Text= established that the circumvallate, or fungiform papillae are the only
#Text= ones concerned in the special sense of taste.
#Text=The conditions necessary to taste are, that the substance be in solution
#Text= either by artificial means, or by the action of the saliva; and that it
#Text= be brought in contact with the sensitive filaments imbedded in the
#Text=mucous membrane.
#Text=The nerves of taste are both _general_ and _special_ in
#Text= their functions.
#Text=If the general sensibility of the nerves of taste is
#Text= unduly excited, the function of sensibility is lost for some time.
#Text=If a
#Text= peppermint lozenge is taken into the mouth, it strongly excites the
#Text= general sensibilities of taste, and the power of distinguishing between
#Text= special flavors is lost for a few moments.
#Text=A nauseous drug may then be
#Text= swallowed without experiencing any disagreeable taste.
#Text=Paralysis of the facial nerve often produces a marked effect in the
#Text= sensibility of the tongue.
#Text=Where this influence lies has not been fully
#Text= explained; probably it is indirect, being produced by some alteration in
#Text= the vascularity of the parts or a diminution of the salivary secretions.
#Text=TOUCH.
#Text=By the sense of touch, we mean the _general sensibility of the skin_.
#Text=Sensations of heat and cold are familiar illustrations of this faculty.
#Text=By the sense of touch, we obtain a knowledge of certain qualities of a
#Text=the mouth with secretions, and a story with unsavory associations may
#Text= completely turn the stomach.
#Text=The relationship of mental and physical functions may be illustrated by
#Text= entirely removing the spleen of an animal, as that of a dog.
#Text=An
#Text= invariable result of its extirpation is an unusual increase of the
#Text= appetite, for at times the animal will eat voraciously any kind of food.
#Text=The dog will devour, with avidity, the warm entrails of recently killed
#Text= animals, and thrive in consequence of such an appetite.
#Text=Another symptom,
#Text= which usually follows the removal of the spleen, is an unnatural
#Text= ferocity of disposition.
#Text=Without any apparent provocation, the animal
#Text= will attack others of its own, or of a different species.
#Text=In some
#Text= instances, these outbursts of irritability and violence are only
#Text= occasional, but the experiments show quite conclusively that the spleen
#Text= moderates combativeness, restrains the appetite, and co-operates with
#Text= the will and judgment in controlling them.
#Text=We shall briefly consider the practical question whether the elements of
#Text= mind can be ideally arranged and presented, so as to more completely
#Text= reveal their relations to, and disclose their effects upon the bodily
#Text=source of recklessness, quarrels, frauds, falsehoods, robberies, and
#Text= homicides.
#Text=They are unlike instinct, inasmuch as they are not
#Text= self-limiting.
#Text=The intimate relation which they sustain to the stomach
#Text= and nutritive functions is strikingly displayed in the habit of
#Text= alcoholic intoxication.
#Text=Spirituous drinks deprave the appetite, derange
#Text= and destroy the stomach, poison the blood, and pervert all the functions
#Text= of mind and body; and their injurious influence upon the nerves and
#Text= basilar faculties is equally remarkable.
#Text=They excite combativeness,
#Text= selfishness, irritability, and exaggerate the influence of the animal
#Text= organs.
#Text=Intemperance results in disputes, fights, brawls, and
#Text= murders--the legitimate consequences of which are misunderstandings,
#Text= suits at law, criminal proceedings, imprisonment, and the gallows.
#Text=It
#Text= is, therefore, evident that the ultimate tendencies of these faculties
#Text= are tyrannical, cruel, violent, and atrocious.
#Text=They are opposed to the
#Text= noble, moral faculties--Faith, Love, and Devotion--and, whenever
#Text= temptation inordinately allures, the course of life is likely to be
#Text= characterized by dishonorable, deceptive, and treacherous conduct.
#Text=The pangs of hunger cause soldiers to act more like ravenous beasts,
#Text= than rational beings.
#Text=It is animal instinct which impels the soldier to
#Text=seek first for the gratification of his appetite.
#Text=Some persons,
#Text= instigated by carnivorous desires, yearn for raw meat, and will not be
#Text= satisfied unless their food is flavored with the flesh of animals.
#Text=Their
#Text= bodies increase and thrive, even to repletion.
#Text=Contrast these
#Text= individuals with pale, lean, anæmic people, who crave innutritious
#Text= articles of diet, and eat soft stones, slate, chalk, blue clay, and soft
#Text= coal.
#Text=Such perversions of the appetite are manifested only when there is
#Text= either a diminution in the volume of blood, deficient alimentation,
#Text= defective assimilation, or a general depravity of the nutritive
#Text= functions.
#Text=Morbid conditions generate vitiating tendencies and destroy
#Text= the natural appetite.
#Text=While alcoholic stimulants affect the medulla oblongata principally,
#Text= opium acts chiefly on the cerebrum, and excites reverie, dreamy
#Text= ideality, optical delusions, and the creative powers of the imagination;
#Text= some of these hallucinations are said to be grotesquely beautiful and
#Text= enjoyable.
#Text=The effects of this agent differ from those of alcoholic
#Text= intoxication by not deadening the moral sensibilities, or arousing the
#Text= animal propensities.
#Text=Opium smokers are dreamy and abstracted, not
#Text= quarrelsome or violent.
#Text=Those who use ardent spirits lose their moral
#Text=delicacy, their intellect becomes dull, the reason cloudy, and the
#Text= judgment is overruled by appetite.
#Text=It is conceded that the _trophic
#Text= center_ is principally in the medulla oblongata; the cerebellum and
#Text= lower cerebral ganglia, however, favorably influence the nutritive
#Text= functions, and, when these organs are large and active, a plethoric
#Text= condition is the natural consequence.
#Text=Redundancy of blood in the body
#Text= indicates preponderance of the basilar organs.
#Text=These faculties being
#Text= vehement in character, an excess of animal characteristics produces
#Text= those conditions which result in acute and inflammatory diseases.

#Text=SOUPS.
#Text=The nutritious properties, tone, and sweetness of soup depend in
#Text= the first place upon the freshness and quality of the meat; secondly on
#Text= the manner in which it is boiled.
#Text=Soups should be nicely and delicately
#Text= seasoned, according to the taste of the consumer, by using parsley,
#Text= sage, savory, thyme, sweet marjoram, sweet basil, or any of the
#Text= vegetable condiments.
#Text=These may be raised in the garden, or obtained at
#Text= the drug stores, sifted and prepared for use.
#Text=In extracting the juices
#Text= of meats, in order that soups may be most nutritious, it is important
#Text= that the meat be put into _cold_ water, or that which is not so hot as
#Text= to coagulate the albumen (which would prevent it from being extracted),
#Text= and then, by slow heat and a simmering process, the most nutritious
#Text= properties will be brought out.
#Text=BEEF SOUP may be made of any bone of the beef, by putting it into cold
#Text= water, adding a little salt, and skimming it well just before it boils.
#Text=If a vegetable flavor be desired, celery, carrots, onions, turnips,
#Text= cabbage, or potatoes, may be added, in sufficient quantities to suit the
#Text= taste.
#Text=MUTTON SOUP may be made from the fore-quarter, in the same manner as
#Text=described above, thickened with pearl-barley or rice, and flavored to
#Text= suit the taste.
#Text=BOILED FISH.
#Text=Clean the fish nicely, then sprinkle flour on a cloth and
#Text= wrap it around them; salt the water, and, when it boils, put in the
#Text= fish; let them boil half an hour, then carefully remove them to a
#Text= platter, adding egg sauce and parsley.
#Text=To _bake fish_, prepare by
#Text= cleaning, scaling, etc., and let them remain in salt water for a short
#Text= time.
#Text=Make a stuffing of the crumbs of light bread, and add to it a
#Text= little salt, pepper, butter, and sweet herbs, and stir with a spoon.
#Text=Then fill the fish with the stuffing and sew it up.
#Text=Put on butter, salt,
#Text= pepper, and flour, having enough water in the dish to keep it from
#Text= burning, and baste often.
#Text=A four pound fish will bake in fifty or sixty
#Text= minutes.
#Text=BROILED STEAK.
#Text=Sirloin and porter-house steaks should be broiled
#Text= quickly.
#Text=Preserve them on ice for a day or two and their tenderness is
#Text= much increased.
#Text=Never broil them until the meal is ready to be served.
#Text=BOILED HEAT.
#Text=When meat is to be boiled for _eating,_ put it into boiling
#Text=water, by which its juices are coagulated and its richness preserved.
#Text=The slower it boils, the more tender, plump, and white it will be.
#Text=Meat
#Text= should be removed as soon as done, or it will lose its flavor and become
#Text= soggy.
#Text=PORK STEAKS.
#Text=The best steaks are cut off the shoulder--ham steaks being
#Text= rather too dry.
#Text=They should be well fried, in order to destroy the
#Text= little living parasites, called Trichinae which sometimes infest this
#Text= kind of meat.
#Text=They are introduced into the stomach by eating ham, pork,
#Text= or sausages made from the flesh of hogs infested by them.
#Text=Thorough
#Text= cooking destroys them, and those who will persist in the use of swine  '  s
#Text= flesh can afford to have it "_done brown._"
#Text=
#Text= BAKED MUTTON.
#Text=To bake mutton well, a person should have a brisk, sharp
#Text= fire, and keep the meat well basted.
#Text=It requires two hours to bake a leg
#Text= of mutton, weighing eight pounds.

#Text= on good, well-baked bread.
#Text=At all events, our enjoyment would be greater
#Text= if it were only better prepared.

#Text=DISTILLED LIQUORS.
#Text=These are whiskey, brandy, and the kindred
#Text= productions of the still.
#Text=Whiskey is a solution of alcohol in water,
#Text= mixed with various other principles which impart to it peculiar physical
#Text= properties.
#Text=The amount of alcohol which it contains varies from
#Text= forty-eight to fifty-six per cent.
#Text=Old whiskey is more highly prized
#Text= than the more recent product of the still, from the fact that when kept
#Text= for some years certain volatile oils are generated which, impart to it a
#Text= mellowness of flavor.
#Text=Brandy is a solution of alcohol in water, together with various other
#Text= substances.
#Text=It contains from fifty to fifty-six per cent. of alcohol.
#Text=Pure brandy is distilled from wine, 1,000 gallons of wine yielding from
#Text= 100 to 150 gallons of brandy, but a very large proportion of the brandy
#Text= is made with little or no wine.
#Text=It is made artificially from high wines
#Text= by the addition of oil of Cognac, to give it flavor, burnt sugar to give
#Text= it color, and logwood or catechu, to impart astringency and roughness of
#Text= taste.
#Text=The best brandy is obtained by distillation from the best quality
#Text= of white wines, from the districts of Cognac and Armagnac in France.

#Text= _Gentlemen_--"A few of my symptoms were: Heartburn and fullness after
#Text= eating, sometimes pain in my bowels, headache, poor appetite and bad
#Text= taste in my mouth.
#Text=My appetite was gone,
#Text= mind and sight impaired, strength and flesh all gone.
#Text=I was a pitiable
#Text= object to look at, divested of all that made life endurable for me.
#Text=I
#Text= had baffled the skill of two physicians, and was left, after three years
#Text=of agony, to die, a "hopeless wreck," worse than death.
#Text=Such was my condition when I applied to you for treatment.
#Text=After using
#Text= medicines only six days I began to improve; my nerves were steadier;
#Text= circulation better, hands and feet warm.
#Text=Nine days after taking your
#Text= medicines they restored the function again.
#Text=I will confess I expected to
#Text= suffer death again--I did not think the medicines had had time to effect
#Text= a change within so short a time.
#Text=Imagine my joy and surprise upon waking
#Text= next morning to find it had "stolen like a thief upon me in the night,"
#Text= I knew not when.
#Text=I spent the day in grateful tears--how could I help it?
#Text=It passed off as quietly as it came, leaving my head clear of that
#Text= _dreadful, burning pressure_!
#Text=My nerves were steady; indeed, my
#Text= improvement was so remarkable, that it seemed almost a delusion.
#Text=My
#Text= appetite had returned, and I was hungry for the first time in over a
#Text= year.
#Text=I slept well--awoke refreshed and feeling stronger.
#Text=After two
#Text= weeks, I was able to walk around the house and yard without support; a
#Text= day or two after that I walked a hundred yards, visiting and spent the
#Text= day.
#Text=In three weeks time I went home (I had gone to my mother  '  s before
#Text= treatment, as I and many others thought, to die).
#Text=At the end of one month there was no symptom, nor sign, of the old
#Text= disease.
#Text=I was able to be up all day, resting a short time at noon.
#Text=To
#Text= be sure of permanent results I continued treatment for one month longer,
#Text= and have never had a return of the disease nor any symptom of it since.
#Text=Before the end of the second month, I was able to be about the house,
#Text= helping the children with the cooking, and milking.
#Text=My weight increased
#Text= fourteen pounds in five months after treatment.
#Text=I have taken no medicine
#Text= since except one bottle of Dr.
#Text=Pierce  '  s Favorite Prescription, four
#Text= years ago.
#Text=At this time (nine years after treatment), I find my health
#Text= still good, having no aches nor pains, a splendid appetite, sleep well,
#Text= no headache, no backache and no womb trouble.
#Text=I am able to do my house
#Text= work and everything; can do a day  '  s work with less fatigue than I have
#Text= for years before treatment.
#Text=I feel sure that I would have been in the
#Text= grave years ago if it had not been for your medicines.
#Text=I advise all
#Text= other ladies who are troubled with the same disease to apply to you for
#Text= treatment.
#Text=Be assured, that whenever I have it in my power I shall recommend your
#Text= invaluable remedies.
#Text=I thank you a thousand times for what you have done
#Text= for me, and for the kindness which you have extended to me throughout.
